app.question: If I land at this spot on the Moon on this date, will I have sunlight and a signal to Earth?
app.intro: Pick a site and a date. We show where the Sun (energy for solar panels) and the Earth (radio communication) are, as seen from there.
selector.timeHint: Universal time (UTC), the same everywhere in the world.
panel.sun.why: Energy: light for the solar panels
help.title: What do these numbers mean?
help.elevation.text: How many degrees it is above the horizon. 0° is right on the horizon and 90° is straight overhead. If it is below the horizon, you cannot see it.
help.azimuth.text: Which way to look, like on a compass: 0° is north, 90° east, 180° south and 270° west.
help.horizon.text: The Sun and the Earth are not points but disks. "Peeking out" means only part of the disk is above the horizon.
help.why.text: At the Moon's south pole the Sun and the Earth stay very close to the horizon: any mountain can hide them. No Sun means no energy, and no Earth in view means no direct communication.
dial.hint: Turn toward the compass direction, then raise your eyes to the height the ruler shows.
view3d.hint: You are standing at the landing site: drag to look around and use the wheel to zoom. The Sun and the Earth are drawn larger than in reality so you can see them; the arc with degrees shows how high they are.
dial.compassSub: View from above: which way to turn?
dial.rulerSub: Side view: how high to look?
help.dials.text: The compass (seen from above) tells you which way to turn: north is up. The ruler tells you how high to look: 0° is the horizon and 90° is straight above your head.

compare.title: Compare scenarios
compare.intro: Choose 2 or 3 site and date combinations and compare their hours of Sun and of Earth in view: the same site on another date, or another site.

live.hint: Decimal degrees: planetocentric latitude from -90 to 90 and east-positive longitude from -180 to 180. The relief comes from NASA's LOLA map: the first query of a point can take up to half a minute.

sky.aria: Sky view from the site: the Sun and the Earth over the horizon
welcome.description: Pick a place on the Moon and a date: the app draws the site's horizon with the Sun and Earth above it and answers one key question: if I land here, will I have sunlight and be able to communicate with Earth? It shows the hours of light, the hours with Earth in view and how long until they set. The data comes from NASA's JPL Horizons.

info.azimuthHelp: Direction to look along the horizon, in degrees: 0° is north and it grows clockwise (90° east, 180° south, 270° west).
info.elevationHelp: Height of the disc's center above the horizon, in degrees: 0° is the horizon and 90° the zenith (straight up). Negative means below the horizon.
info.stateHelp: Whether the body can be seen from there: above the horizon (whole disc), peeking (only the top edge), hidden by the terrain (above the flat horizon, but a mountain blocks it) or below the horizon (not visible).
info.nextHelp: When the body first crosses the horizon after the chosen moment: set if it hides, rise if it appears. Estimated by interpolation (± a few minutes).
info.countdownHelp: Time left until that next change (set or rise). It runs live from the chosen moment.
info.radiusHelp: Apparent size of each disc as seen from the Moon (radius, in degrees). These are fixed nominal values from the data contract: Sun 0.25° and Earth 1.0°. In reality they vary slightly with distance (Earth between ~0.9° and ~1.05°), but we do not compute it per sample; the effect on when each body is visible is minimal.
info.windows: Visible hours from the selected time
info.next24hHelp: Hours, out of the next 24, in which the body is above the horizon. “Both” counts hours with the Sun and Earth up at once.
info.next7dHelp: Hours, out of the next 7 days, in which the body is above the horizon. “Both” counts hours with the Sun and Earth up at once.
info.next30dHelp: Hours, out of the next 30 days, in which the body is above the horizon. “Both” counts hours with the Sun and Earth up at once.
info.sunVisibleHelp: Hours in the period when the Sun is above the horizon: there is light for solar panels. In parentheses, the share of the period.
info.earthVisibleHelp: Hours in the period when Earth is above the horizon: there is line of sight for communications. In parentheses, the share of the period.
info.bothVisibleHelp: Hours with both solar power and communication with Earth: the best time to operate.
info.noneVisibleHelp: Hours with neither sunlight nor communication with Earth: the worst case, only batteries keep things alive.
info.longestNoSunHelp: The longest continuous stretch in the period with the Sun below the horizon: the longest night to endure.
info.longestNoEarthHelp: The longest continuous stretch in the period without Earth above the horizon: the longest time without direct communication.
info.longestNoBothHelp: The longest continuous stretch in the period without both Sun and Earth up together (at least one of them is missing).
info.note: Ideal horizon, no terrain (ADR-011). Visible: the upper edge of the disc is above the horizon. Hourly data from JPL Horizons; crossings are interpolated (± a few minutes).
info.noteRelief: Real LOLA terrain. Visible: the upper edge of the disc is above the horizon. Hourly data from JPL Horizons; crossings are interpolated (± a few minutes).
